title: Thyroid Functional Alterations and Autoimmunity According to Serum Vitamin B12 and Folic Acid Concentrations: A Population-Based Case–Control Study
content: Background/Objectives: Vitamin B12 and folic acid participate in one-carbon metabolism and immune regulation, but their relationship with autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD) and thyroid dysfunction remains inconsistently reported. This study aimed to determine the sociodemographic and clinical characteristics and to establish whether serum vitamin B12 and folic acid concentrations are associated with thyroid function and with thyroid autoantibody (TPOAb, TgAb, TRAb) positivity. Methods: A population-based case–control study was conducted among adults, comprising 728 AITD cases and 728 age/sex/BMI/socioeconomic-status/origin-matched healthy controls (N = 1456). AITD was defined by positivity for at least one of three thyroid autoantibodies; thyroid function was classified from thyrotropin (TSH) and free thyroxine (FT4). Serum vitamin B12 and folic acid were categorized using clinical reference cut-offs; group comparisons used Student's t-test, chi-square/Fisher's exact tests, and binary logistic regression with receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Results: Vitamin B12 deficiency was more prevalent among cases than controls (32.0% vs. 9.5%; p < 0.001), and vitamin B12 deficiency independently predicted thyroid dysfunction (OR: 2.50, 95% CI: 1.89‒3.30) and positivity for all three autoantibodies (OR: 2.0–2.5). Folic acid deficiency was less prevalent (4.9%) and showed no independent effect in any adjusted model. Goiter, subclinical/overt hypothyroidism, and autoantibody positivity were all significantly more frequent among cases. Discriminative models combining vitamin B12 and folic acid categories showed modest predictive capacity (AUC 0.58–0.59). Conclusions: In this population-based case–control study, vitamin B12 deficiency—far more than folic acid status—was consistently associated with thyroid dysfunction and with AITD, supporting vitamin B12 assessment as a reasonable, low-cost adjunct in the clinical evaluation of AITD, while highlighting the modest standalone discriminative capacity of these nutritional markers.
